title: The Stanford Multifaceted Dissociation Questionnaire: A 9-Item Measure of Trait and State Dissociation.
abstract: Dissociation is a common and increasingly studied phenomenon with substantial relevance for mental health. To date, researchers have often relied upon broad conceptualizations and retrospective measures, making it difficult to identify a consistent subset of experiences for dissociation, explore their links to related phenomena, and differentiate habitual from momentary dissociation. To address these issues, we introduce the Stanford Multifaceted Dissociation Questionnaire (SMDQ), a 9-item measure that assesses three facets of dissociation and can be employed to assess either trait or state dissociation. In Study 1, we evaluated the content validity of the initial SMDQ item pool using feedback from individuals with lived experience of dissociation (N = 73) and content experts (N = 14), detailing our focus on detachment-type experiences that may help the dissociation construct to be more cleanly distinguished from other clinical phenomena. In Study 2 (N = 400), we described the item selection process and examined the factor structure, internal consistency, and convergent/discriminant validity of both the trait and state versions of the SMDQ. In Study 3 (N = 500), we further investigated the psychometric properties of both versions, including their factor structure, measurement invariance, internal consistency, test-retest reliability, and convergent/discriminant validity. Across the studies, scores on the trait and state versions of the SMDQ showed strong content validity and a theoretically congruent factor structure, comprised of alteration in the perception of one's mind, body, and world (suggesting a tripartite model of dissociation). This structure was largely invariant across demographic groups and time. We also demonstrate good convergent and discriminant validity, internal consistency (ω > 0.80), and temporal stability over 1 week (r > 0.70 for the trait version). Overall, we conclude that the trait and state versions of the SMDQ are promising measurement tools that can enhance our understanding of dissociation's structure, antecedents, and consequences.
